newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - FORECAST - Australian imports to bounce in August.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - FORECAST - Australian imports to bounce in August.

text.p: Australia's imports bill looks set to record a modest rise in August, but economists said Wednesday's data should contain little to alarm markets after the weakness seen in the series in recent months.

The underlying trend in imports remains weak, but economists said that after three consecutive falls, the weakness seen in capital goods seen in the last two months, the expected inclusion of an aircraft and a fall in the Australian dollar during the month all pointed to a bounce in August.
The median forecast of the 28 economists Reuters surveyed was for a 2.2 percent rise. Forecasts ranged from a 1.0 percent fall to a 5.0 percent rise, with only three economists forecasting a fall.
Imports have fallen in each of the last three months, to be down a total of 8.0 percent.
"Merchandise imports are forecast to post a modest 2.0 percent rise in August after three consecutive monthly declines," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
"However, the broader trend is expected to remain one of slowing import growth," he said.
Economists said various factors suggested a rise, not least of which was some statistical volatility in the series.
As well, the expected inclusion of an aircraft plane worth about A$100 million should boost the August billl.

"The August imports data will contain an aircraft and should reflect some kind of rebound from the exaggerated weakness, in relation to other partial indicators, of recent months," Bain and Company economists said in a commentary.

The median forecast of a 2.2 percent rise would still leave imports at their second lowest level thos year, and if it fell by the 1.0 percent some have forecast, it would be the smallest imports bill since last October.

On the other hand, if the highest forecast of a 5.0 percent rise was realised, imports would be at their highest level in the past three months but would remain over four percent under their 1996 peak recorded in February.
Of the three import categories -- consumption, capital and intermediate goods -- capital goods were expected to be the strongest in August.
Capital goods have fallen heavily in the last two months, by a total of 22.7 percent, and many economists expected a corrective rise.
Such weakness sits at odds with official expectations of strong business investment, which should show up in capital good imports, economists said.

The recently reported strong 2.4 percent rise in July retail trade may be a pointer to weaker consumer imports. The retail data was given a big boost by department store clearance sales, and economists said stores may have been running down their inventories and not ordering in new stock just yet.
